title: Derivatives
intro: A derivative is the rate at which one quantity changes with another at a single point: the slope of the tangent line.

blocks.text: From average speed to instantaneous speed

A dropped stone has fallen about $s(t) = 5t^2$ metres after $t$ seconds (using $g \approx 10$ metres per second squared and ignoring air). How fast is it moving at $t = 2$? Average speed over the next $h$ seconds is distance covered divided by time taken:
With $h = 1$ this is 25 metres per second. With $h = 0.1$ it is 20.5, with $h = 0.01$ it is 20.05, and with $h = 0.001$ it is 20.005. The averages close in on 20. Algebra shows why:
As $h$ approaches 0 the limit is 20. We could not just set $h = 0$ at the start, because that gives $0/0$. The limit (#/math/calculus/limits) is what makes the step legal.
The definition
The derivative of $f$ at $x$, written $f'(x)$ or $\frac{df}{dx}$, is

when that limit exists. A function with a derivative at a point is called differentiable there. The units are the units of $f$ divided by the units of $x$: metres per second here, volts per second for a voltage that changes in time.
The picture: secants become the tangent

On the graph of $f$, the fraction is the slope of the straight line through two points on the curve, at $x$ and at $x + h$. That line is a secant. As $h$ shrinks, the second point slides towards the first and the secant turns towards the tangent line, the line that matches the curve's direction at that point.

widget.title: Secants closing on the tangent of x²

blocks.text: At the starting setting, $a = 1$ and $h = 1$, the secant has slope 3 and the tangent slope 2. Drag $h$ down: the secant slope reads 2.50 at $h = 0.5$, 2.10 at $h = 0.1$ and 2.01 at $h = 0.01$, and the two lines merge. Then move $a$ and watch the tangent slope stay at twice $a$.
Deriving a rule: the derivative of x²

So $f'(x) = 2x$: not one number but a new function that gives the slope at every point. At $x = 1$ the slope is 2, at $x = 0$ it is 0 (the bottom of the parabola), and at $x = -3$ it is $-6$ (falling steeply).
The rules you will use
Nobody takes the limit afresh each time. A few results, each proved from the definition, cover most functions:

items: Power: the derivative of $x^n$ is $n x^{n-1}$ for any real $n$ (for negative or fractional $n$, where the expressions are defined).
Constant multiple and sum: $(c f)' = c f'$ and $(f + g)' = f' + g'$.
Exponential and logarithm: the derivative of $e^x$ is $e^x$, and that of $\ln x$ is $1/x$ for $x > 0$.
Sine and cosine, in radians: the derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$, and that of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$.
Product: $(f g)' = f' g + f g'$.
Quotient: $(f / g)' = (f' g - f g') / g^2$, where $g \neq 0$.
Chain: the derivative of $f(g(x))$ is $f'(g(x))\, g'(x)$.

blocks.text: The chain rule, slowly

The chain rule handles a function inside a function. If $u$ changes 3 times as fast as $x$, and $y$ changes 4 times as fast as $u$, then $y$ changes $4 \times 3 = 12$ times as fast as $x$: rates multiply.

For $y = (3x + 1)^2$, the inner function is $u = 3x + 1$ with $u' = 3$, and the outer is $u^2$ with derivative $2u$. So $y' = 2(3x+1) \cdot 3 = 18x + 6$. Expanding first gives $y = 9x^2 + 6x + 1$ and the same derivative.
For $y = e^{-5t}$ the inner function is $-5t$, so $y' = -5 e^{-5t}$. A quantity that decays exponentially changes at a rate proportional to how much is left.
Using the derivative
Straight-line approximation

Near $x = a$ the tangent line is a good stand-in for the function: $f(a + h) \approx f(a) + f'(a) h$. To estimate $\sqrt{4.1}$, take $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ with $a = 4$. The power rule with $n = \frac{1}{2}$ gives $f'(x) = \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{x}}$, so $f'(4) = \frac{1}{4}$. The estimate is $2 + 0.1 / 4 = 2.025$. The true value is 2.02485.
Highest and lowest points

At a smooth peak or valley inside an interval the tangent is flat, so $f'(x) = 0$. Suppose you have 40 metres of fence for a rectangle. Two widths and two lengths use the 40 metres, so width plus length is 20. With width $w$ the length is $20 - w$ and the area is $A(w) = 20w - w^2$. Then $A'(w) = 20 - 2w$, which is zero at $w = 10$. The slope is positive before and negative after, so this is a maximum: a square of area 100 square metres.
A zero derivative is a candidate, not a proof. $x^3$ has slope 0 at $x = 0$ but is neither a peak nor a valley there. Check the sign of $f'$ on both sides, and check the ends of the interval too.
Second derivatives

Differentiating the derivative gives the second derivative $f''$, the rate of change of the rate of change. For position it is acceleration. For the falling stone $s' = 10t$ and $s'' = 10$, the constant acceleration we started with.
When there is no derivative

$|x|$ is continuous at 0 but has a sharp corner: the slope is $-1$ from the left and $1$ from the right, so the limit that defines the derivative does not exist. A jump also rules out a derivative, and so does a vertical tangent, as for the cube root at 0. Every differentiable function is continuous, but not the other way round.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Power and sum
blocks.text: Differentiate $f(x) = 3x^4 - 2x + 7$.
solution: Apply the power rule term by term: $3 \cdot 4x^3 - 2 + 0$.

blocks.title: Product
blocks.text: Differentiate $f(x) = x^2 e^x$.
solution: Product rule: $(x^2)' e^x + x^2 (e^x)' = 2x e^x + x^2 e^x$.

blocks.title: Chain
blocks.text: Differentiate $f(t) = \sin(2 \pi t)$.
solution: The inner function is $2\pi t$ with derivative $2\pi$.

blocks.title: Fastest rise
blocks.text: A capacitor voltage is $v(t) = 5 (1 - e^{-t/2})$ volts, with $t$ in seconds. How fast is it rising at $t = 0$?
solution: Write $v(t) = 5 - 5 e^{-t/2}$. By the chain rule the derivative of $e^{-t/2}$ is $-\frac{1}{2} e^{-t/2}$, so $v'(t) = -5 \cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) e^{-t/2} = \frac{5}{2} e^{-t/2}$.
At $t = 0$ this is 2.5 volts per second, and it only gets slower afterwards.
